name: Flaxseed oil
short: Observational, alpha-linolenic acid not flaxseed oil: weak prostate cancer link, significant by type only in blood/tissue; none after bias adjustment. Rheumatoid arthritis trial: longer bleeding time.
text: Few safety data on flaxseed oil itself were found. On cancer, a meta-analysis of 8 case-control and 8 prospective observational studies of alpha-linolenic acid (the omega-3 fat found in flaxseed oil) measured as dietary intake or blood and tissue levels, not trials of flaxseed oil, found a weak association between high levels and prostate cancer (relative risk 1.20); when examined by study type, only the six observational studies that measured alpha-linolenic acid in blood or tissue (not flaxseed oil intake) showed a statistically significant association, the remaining studies showed significant heterogeneity and evidence of publication bias, and after adjustment for publication bias there was no overall association (relative risk 0.96). The authors called the findings inconsistent and concluded that high intakes or high blood and tissue levels of alpha-linolenic acid may be associated with a small increased risk of prostate cancer, a conclusion they qualified because of differences between studies and likely publication bias. In a 3-month placebo-controlled trial of alpha-linolenic acid in 22 people with rheumatoid arthritis (titled flaxseed versus safflower seed), the treatment group showed an increased bleeding time; the abstract reports no bleeding events and does not mention blood-thinning medicines. In a 16-week randomised trial in 51 children and adolescents with bipolar disorder comparing flax oil capsules with an olive oil placebo, the authors concluded that essential fatty acid supplementation was feasible and well tolerated but noted the burden of the number of capsules; the abstract does not list adverse events. A case report described a 70-year-old man who developed painful breast swelling three months after starting a daily tablespoon of flaxseed oil; a biopsy showed gynaecomastia without cancer, and the authors discussed a possible role of plant oestrogens. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
